title: Find employees who do NOT belong to any of the given departments (use `!Set.contains`).
shortTitle: Find employees who do NOT belong to any of the given departments (use !Set.contains)

s1_definition.profdef: This is a negated membership `filter`. You hold the excluded departments in a `Set<String>` and the predicate is `e -> !excluded.contains(e.getDepartment())`, which keeps an element only when its department is NOT in the set. A `HashSet` gives average constant-time lookup, making this efficient even for large exclusion lists.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR manager at the National Bank of India has a short blacklist of departments pinned to the wall — say IT and HR. She is told, "Give me everyone who is NOT in any of those." She checks each person's department against the pinned list; if it is on the list she skips them, otherwise she keeps them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put the unwanted values in a Set and filter with NOT contains to keep everything outside that set.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a negated membership `filter`. You hold the excluded departments in a `Set<String>` and the predicate is `e -> !excluded.contains(e.getDepartment())`, which keeps an element only when its department is NOT in the set. A `HashSet` gives average constant-time lookup, making this efficient even for large exclusion lists.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR manager at the National Bank of India has a short blacklist of departments pinned to the wall — say IT and HR. She is told, "Give me everyone who is NOT in any of those." She checks each person's department against the pinned list; if it is on the list she skips them, otherwise she keeps them.

**One line to remember:** Put the unwanted values in a Set and filter with NOT contains to keep everything outside that set.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Set` is a collection with no duplicates and a very fast `contains` check. The `contains(Object)` method returns true when the element is present. Negating it with the logical NOT operator flips the meaning, so `!excluded.contains(dept)` is true exactly when the department is absent from the excluded set.

Using a `Set` rather than a `List` for the exclusion check matters for performance. `List.contains` scans every element in linear time, so filtering a large employee list against a large exclusion list becomes slow. `HashSet.contains` is average constant time because it hashes the value and jumps straight to the bucket. For banking datasets with thousands of records this difference is real.

Inside the stream the predicate reads `e -> !excluded.contains(e.getDepartment())`. The method reference style is not natural here because of the negation, so a lambda is clearest. You can also express it as `excluded.contains(dept) == false`, but the NOT operator is idiomatic.

A senior nuance: build the set once, outside the stream, not inside the predicate, otherwise you would rebuild it for every element. Also consider case: if department casing is inconsistent you normalise both the set contents and the compared value to the same case.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is rolling out a new field-sales training. The learning team says the training is for everyone EXCEPT the back-office departments, which they list as IT and HR, because those teams get a different technical course. HR has the full staff list and needs everyone whose department is not in that excluded set. This is exactly how a negated set-membership filter works — each employee's department is checked against the excluded set, and only those NOT in it are kept.

The code defines an `Employee` with name and department. A `TrainingService` holds the excluded departments in a `Set` and exposes `eligibleForFieldTraining(List<Employee>)` filtering with NOT contains. The runnable `Main` feeds employees across several departments and logs who is eligible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (IT), Priya (Sales), Amit (HR), Neha (Marketing), Karan (Sales). Excluded set: IT, HR.

Step 1: The stream opens over five employees. The excluded set was built once before the stream.

Step 2: Rajesh enters. The set contains IT, so contains returns true, NOT true is false — Rajesh is dropped.

Step 3: Priya enters. The set does not contain Sales, so contains is false, NOT false is true — Priya passes.

Step 4: Amit enters. The set contains HR, so NOT contains is false — Amit dropped.

Step 5: Neha enters. Marketing is not in the set — passes.

Step 6: Karan enters. Sales is not in the set — passes.

Step 7: `collect` gathers Priya, Neha, Karan.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find elements that do not belong to a group of values, I keep the unwanted values in a Set and filter with a negated contains, so an element survives only when its value is absent from that set. The predicate is simply NOT of the set's contains method on the employee's department, which reads naturally as "keep this person if their department is not in the excluded list."

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was the field-sales training rollout. The learning team wanted everyone except the back-office departments, which they listed as IT and HR, so I held those two in an excluded set and streamed the staff list, keeping only employees whose department was not in that set. The remaining Sales, Marketing, and other field staff became eligible.

A senior point I always stress is to use a Set, not a List, for the exclusion check, and to build it once outside the stream. A set's contains is average constant time because it hashes straight to the bucket, whereas a list's contains scans every element linearly, so for a large exclusion list against thousands of employees the set is dramatically faster. I also build the set a single time as a constant rather than inside the predicate, because rebuilding it for every employee would waste work, and if department casing were inconsistent in the data I would normalise both the set contents and the compared value to the same case so the membership test stays correct.
